intro: The first two books of the Torah tell of a family and a rescue. The last three turn that rescued people into a community with a way of life. Leviticus sets out offerings, purity and holiness. Numbers counts the tribes and follows them through forty years in the wilderness. Deuteronomy gives Moses's last speeches, ending with his death within sight of the land. Jewish tradition reads these books as Vayikra, Bamidbar and Devarim, and draws from them the Shema, Yom Kippur, tzedakah and the 613 commandments.

Then the story crosses the Jordan. The books Jewish tradition calls the Former Prophets, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, tell one long history: the land taken and settled, the judges, the first kings, David's Jerusalem and Solomon's Temple, a kingdom split in two, prophets who confront kings, and two empires, Assyria and Babylon, that end it. The text judges every king by the standard Deuteronomy set.

In this unit you will read laws and stories side by side and see how each shapes the other. You will meet the commentators and the rabbis who have read these books for two thousand years, and the historians and archaeologists who set the text beside stones and clay from the ground. You will be able to explain what a passage says, how Jewish tradition has read it, and what the outside evidence adds.
bigQuestion: How do law, story and history work together in the Torah's last books and the Former Prophets to explain who Israel is and why its kingdom fell?

timeline.t: The Merneptah Stele in Egypt names "Israel" as a people in Canaan
Small villages spread through the central hill country, read by many as early Israel
David reigns; the text says he makes Jerusalem his capital
The kingdom splits into Israel in the north and Judah in the south
The Mesha Stele from Moab names King Omri of Israel
Assyria takes Samaria and deports the northern kingdom
Sennacherib besieges Jerusalem; the city is not taken
A scroll is found in the Temple and Josiah reforms worship
Babylon captures Jerusalem and exiles King Jehoiachin
Babylon burns the Temple and deports Judah
De Wette links Josiah's scroll with Deuteronomy
The Tel Dan stele naming the "House of David" is found

words.d: the Hebrew name of Leviticus, from its first word, "And He called"
the Day of Atonement described in Leviticus 16; a day of fasting and confession in Jewish practice
scholars' name for Leviticus 17–26, which repeats the call to be holy as God is holy
the Hebrew name of Numbers, meaning "in the wilderness"
the passage beginning "Hear, O Israel" in Deuteronomy 6, said morning and evening in Jewish prayer
giving to those in need; from tzedek, justice, so tradition reads it as something owed
a commandment of the Torah; rabbinic tradition counts 613 (plural: mitzvot)
Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, the first four books of Nevi'im
scholars' name for Joshua through Kings read as one work judged by Deuteronomy's standards
to pour oil on a person's head as a sign of being chosen, as Samuel did for Saul and David

test.q: Which book does Jewish tradition call Vayikra?
test.why: Vayikra, "And He called," is the first word and Hebrew name of Leviticus.

test.q: In Leviticus 16, what did the high priest do with the second goat?
choices: Confessed the people's sins over it and sent it into the wilderness
Offered it at the altar with the first
test.why: Leviticus 16 says the high priest confessed the people's sins over the goat and it was sent away into the wilderness.

test.q: Which verse did Rabbi Akiva call a great principle of the Torah?
test.why: The midrash records Rabbi Akiva calling Leviticus 19:18 a great principle of the Torah.

test.q: Why does the text say the generation that left Egypt did not enter the land?
choices: They believed the fearful report of ten spies and refused to go up
test.why: Numbers 14 says that after the spies' report and the people's weeping, that generation was to wander forty years.

test.q: What did the daughters of Zelophehad win in Numbers 27?
choices: Leadership of the tribe of Manasseh
Their father's share of land, and a new rule for all daughters without brothers
test.why: Numbers 27 says the sisters spoke rightly and received their father's inheritance, and a general rule for daughters followed.

test.q: What does the Hebrew name Devarim mean?
test.why: Devarim means "words," from Deuteronomy's opening, "These are the words which Moses spoke."

test.q: Which object do the rabbis connect to Deuteronomy 6:9, "write them on the doorposts of your house"?
test.why: Rabbinic tradition reads Deuteronomy 6:9 as the source of the mezuzah on a Jewish home's doorpost.

test.q: What reason does Deuteronomy 10:19 give for loving the stranger?
choices: Moses was a stranger in Moab
You were strangers in the land of Egypt
test.why: Deuteronomy ties care for the stranger to the memory of Egypt: you were strangers there.

test.q: Where does the number 613 for the commandments come from?
choices: A teaching of Rabbi Simlai in the Talmud
test.why: The Talmud (Makkot 23b) records Rabbi Simlai's teaching of 613 commandments; Maimonides later listed them.

test.q: Which books does Jewish tradition call the Former Prophets?
choices: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and the Twelve
test.why: The Former Prophets are Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, the first books of Nevi'im.

test.q: What did Kathleen Kenyon's work at Jericho find?
choices: Walls that fell around 1550 BCE, centuries before most dates given to Joshua
A copy of the book of Joshua
test.why: Kenyon's excavations found Jericho's walls had collapsed around 1550 BCE and the site was small or empty later.

test.q: What did the people ask of Samuel in 1 Samuel 8?
choices: A king like the other nations
test.why: The elders asked Samuel for a king like all the nations; Samuel warned them what a king would take.

test.q: About when did the kingdom split into Israel and Judah?
test.why: Historians date the split after Solomon's death to about 930 BCE.

test.q: According to 1 Kings 19, what came after the wind, the earthquake and the fire?
test.why: 1 Kings 19:12 says the LORD was not in the wind, earthquake or fire, and after the fire came a still small voice.

choices: Babylon burned the Temple and deported Judah
The Tel Dan stele was carved
test.why: 2 Kings 25 tells of Babylon burning the Temple and Jerusalem; historians date it to 586 BCE.

write.prompt: The book of Kings says Josiah tore his clothes when a found scroll was read to him, and then reformed worship. Using 2 Kings 22:8–13, 2 Kings 23:1–3 and one passage from Deuteronomy (such as 6:4–9 or 12:5–14), explain what the scroll seems to have demanded and how Jewish tradition and modern scholars each account for the scroll's origin.
tips: Name each passage you cite by book, chapter and verse.
Attribute every reading: "Jewish tradition holds…", "de Wette argued…", "the text says…".
Compare the two accounts of the scroll's origin without deciding which is true.
Use the unit's terms: Deuteronomistic History, covenant, reform, Devarim.
Keep each paragraph to one idea.
